hints: The definition links a body's mass to its velocity.
walkthrough: Linear momentum is found by multiplying mass by velocity.

ai_rubric.observable: Defines linear momentum as mass multiplied by velocity.

hints: The blocks are in contact while block Y's momentum is changing on the graph.
walkthrough: The momentum of block Y starts to increase at 60 ms, indicating the start of contact.
It becomes constant again at 100 ms, indicating that contact has ended.
The contact time is 100 ms − 60 ms = 40 ms.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the contact interval from 60 ms to 100 ms and gives 40 ms.

hints: For a block of constant mass, a straight momentum–time line has a constant gradient, while a horizontal line has zero gradient.
Use the connection between momentum-change rate, force and acceleration to compare the two intervals.
walkthrough: From 80 ms to 100 ms, the momentum–time graph is a straight rising line, so its gradient and hence the rate of momentum change are constant.
For constant mass, constant force means constant acceleration, so the magnitude of the acceleration is constant in this interval.
From 100 ms to 120 ms, the graph is horizontal, so momentum is constant and its rate of change is zero.
The resultant force and therefore the magnitude of the acceleration are zero in this interval.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the magnitude of the acceleration is constant from 80 ms to 100 ms.
States that the magnitude of the acceleration is zero from 100 ms to 120 ms.

hints: Read the change in block Y's momentum and the interval over which that change occurs from Fig. 2.2.
Use force as the rate of change of momentum, and convert the graph time from milliseconds to seconds.
walkthrough: During contact, block Y's momentum increases from 0 to 0.50 kg m s⁻¹ in 40 ms.
The force magnitude is 13 N to two significant figures.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses force as the rate of change of momentum, or the gradient of the momentum–time graph.
Uses a momentum change of 0.50 kg m s⁻¹ over 40 ms to obtain a force magnitude of 13 N.

hints: There is no external horizontal force, so the total momentum of both blocks stays at its initial value.
At each time on block Y's graph, subtract its momentum from 0.40 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain the momentum of block X.
Use the start and end of the sloping section of block Y's graph to set the three corresponding segments for block X.
walkthrough: Initially, the total momentum is 0.40 kg m s⁻¹ because block X has 0.40 kg m s⁻¹ and block Y is stationary. The frictionless surface means this total remains constant.
Before contact, from 0 ms to 60 ms, block Y has zero momentum, so block X remains at +0.40 kg m s⁻¹. Draw a horizontal line from (0, 0.40) to (60, 0.40).
During contact, from 60 ms to 100 ms, block Y's momentum increases linearly from 0 to +0.50 kg m s⁻¹. Block X's momentum must therefore decrease linearly from +0.40 to 0.40 − 0.50 = −0.10 kg m s⁻¹.
After contact, from 100 ms to 160 ms, the two momenta are constant. Draw a horizontal line for block X at −0.10 kg m s⁻¹ from 100 ms to 160 ms.

Draws a straight line for block X from (60 ms, +0.40 kg m s⁻¹) to (100 ms, −0.10 kg m s⁻¹).
Draws a horizontal line for block X from (100 ms, −0.10 kg m s⁻¹) to (160 ms, −0.10 kg m s⁻¹).
